misconceptions.statement: If a message says I won a prize, I must pay a small fee first to get it, and that is normal.
misconceptions.why: Students think fees like taxes or courier charges are part of every genuine prize.
misconceptions.fix: A real prize never needs you to pay money in advance. Asking for a fee to release a prize is the main sign of a lottery scam.

probe.question: A message says you won Rs 10 lakh but must pay Rs 5,000 as processing fee. What should you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Pay the fee because it is small compared to the prize.

misconceptions.root_belief: paying a little first is the normal price of gains

misconceptions.statement: If a message has my name and mobile number, the lottery win must be real.
misconceptions.why: Students think only a real organiser could know their personal details.
misconceptions.fix: Scammers get names and numbers from leaks and lists. Having your name does not make a message genuine, and you cannot win a draw you never entered.

probe.question: You get an SMS with your name saying you won a lucky draw you never joined. Is it real?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it has my name, so they must know me.

misconceptions.root_belief: personal details prove something is genuine

misconceptions.statement: It is worth replying just to check, because replying cannot cause any harm.
misconceptions.why: Students think only paying money or clicking can hurt, not a simple reply.
misconceptions.fix: Replying shows your number is active and invites more targeted scam attempts. It is safest to ignore, block and report such messages.

probe.question: An unknown number says you won a prize. Is it safe to reply 'who are you?'
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, replying is harmless; only paying causes loss.

misconceptions.root_belief: harm needs a big visible action

misconceptions.statement: If a caller says they are from my bank and know my name, I can trust them and share details to update KYC.
misconceptions.why: Students think a caller who sounds official and knows basic facts must be genuine.
misconceptions.fix: Banks never ask for OTP, PIN or card details by phone or link. KYC is updated at the branch or through the bank's own app or website.

probe.question: A caller says your account will be blocked unless you tell the OTP to update KYC. What do you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Tell the OTP so the account does not get blocked.

misconceptions.root_belief: sounding official means being genuine

misconceptions.statement: KYC must be updated within hours by clicking the link sent by SMS, otherwise the account closes immediately.
misconceptions.why: Scare messages with deadlines make students believe the threat is a real bank rule.
misconceptions.fix: Banks give written notice and ample time and do not close accounts through sudden SMS links. Go to the branch or official app instead.

probe.question: An SMS says click this link in 2 hours to update KYC or the account closes. Should you click?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, click quickly to save the account.

misconceptions.root_belief: a deadline means the threat is real

misconceptions.statement: Phishing happens only through emails, not through SMS, WhatsApp or phone calls.
misconceptions.why: The word is usually explained with email examples in books.
misconceptions.fix: Phishing can come through email, SMS, WhatsApp, calls and social media. Any message that tricks you into sharing details or clicking a fake link is phishing.

probe.question: A WhatsApp message has a link to 'claim your electricity refund'. Can it be phishing?
probe.wrong_answer: No, phishing is only done by email.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means only the first example learned

misconceptions.statement: A phishing link can only harm me if I type my password or pay money on the page.
misconceptions.why: Students think only entering details counts as danger.
misconceptions.fix: Some fake links install harmful apps or steal data once opened or downloaded. Do not open or download from unknown links at all.

probe.question: You get a link from an unknown sender. If you only open it and enter nothing, is it always safe?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is only dangerous if I type my password.

misconceptions.root_belief: harm needs a big visible action

misconceptions.statement: A scheme that has been paying its members regular returns for months must be genuine.
misconceptions.why: Students think that seeing payments received proves the business really earns profit.
misconceptions.fix: A Ponzi scheme pays early investors using money from newer investors, so it works until new members stop joining. Then it collapses and most people lose their money.

probe.question: A company paid your neighbour 10% every month for a year. Does this prove it is real?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, getting paid regularly proves it earns real profit.

misconceptions.root_belief: what I have seen working will keep working
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of investor behaviour and regulatory reports on Ponzi and chain-money schemes

misconceptions.statement: Bringing more friends into a scheme is a safe way to earn, because everyone gains.
misconceptions.why: Referral rewards look like a normal business or marketing method.
misconceptions.fix: In schemes that pay members for recruiting others, money only comes from new joiners, so the later ones lose. Such money circulation schemes are illegal in India.

probe.question: A scheme says join and earn more by adding 3 friends. Is everyone sure to gain?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, more members means more earnings for all.

misconceptions.root_belief: more people joining means more gain for all

misconceptions.statement: Police or CBI can put a person under 'digital arrest' on a video call until they pay money.
misconceptions.why: News and films show arrests, so scary video calls from uniformed people seem real.
misconceptions.fix: There is no such thing as digital arrest in Indian law. No agency demands money or arrests people over video call; hang up and call 1930.

probe.question: A video caller in uniform says you are under digital arrest and must transfer money to be cleared. What do you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Obey, because police can arrest anyone on a video call.

misconceptions.root_belief: authority figures must always be obeyed

misconceptions.statement: If a scheme promises high returns with a written guarantee, it is safe.
misconceptions.why: Students trust anything that is written down and looks official.
misconceptions.fix: Genuine investments carry risk, and higher returns usually mean higher risk. A guarantee of very high fixed returns is a classic fraud sign.

probe.question: A firm guarantees 30% profit every month with no risk. Is it safe?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a guarantee means no loss.

misconceptions.root_belief: a promise or paper guarantees the outcome
misconceptions.source_hint: financial literacy surveys and regulator investor-awareness material on high-return fraud

misconceptions.statement: Earning 20% a month is just a good business skill, and banks give low interest only because they are lazy.
misconceptions.why: Students compare bank interest with large offers without thinking how profit is produced.
misconceptions.fix: Bank interest is low because it is safe and based on real lending. Very high steady returns cannot come from any real business, so they signal a scam.

probe.question: Bank gives 7% a year; a scheme gives 20% a month. Which is more trustworthy?
probe.wrong_answer: The scheme, since it gives more money.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger number means a better deal
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of numeracy and financial literacy in investment decisions

misconceptions.statement: If an offer says 'only for today', I should act fast so I don't miss it.
misconceptions.why: Shops use limited-time sales, so urgency seems normal.
misconceptions.fix: Scammers create urgency so you cannot think or ask someone. A genuine offer survives a pause to check it.

probe.question: A caller says pay in 10 minutes or lose the offer. What is the best step?
probe.wrong_answer: Pay immediately so the offer is not lost.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from familiar settings works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: If someone asks me to keep the deal secret from my family, it is only to protect my special chance.
misconceptions.why: Secrecy feels like trust and being chosen.
misconceptions.fix: Scammers ask for secrecy so no one can warn you. Always tell a trusted adult about any money deal.

probe.question: A person says do not tell your parents about this earning offer. What do you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Keep it secret, since it is my special chance.

misconceptions.root_belief: being chosen means being trusted

misconceptions.statement: Messages from unknown people are safe if they come from a number that looks like a normal 10-digit mobile number.
misconceptions.why: Students think scammers use strange numbers or foreign codes only.
misconceptions.fix: Scammers use ordinary mobile numbers and can even fake caller names. Judge the request, not how the number looks.

probe.question: A normal-looking mobile number offers a part-time job paying Rs 5,000 daily for liking videos. Is it safe?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is a normal Indian number.

misconceptions.root_belief: looks normal means it is safe

misconceptions.statement: It is fine to share an OTP with a bank employee because the bank sent it.
misconceptions.why: Students see that the OTP comes from the bank, so they think the bank may ask for it.
misconceptions.fix: An OTP is a secret only for you to enter yourself. No bank or company employee ever needs to ask for it.

probe.question: A caller says they are from your bank and asks for the OTP just received. Should you tell?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the bank sent it so they can have it.

misconceptions.root_belief: the source of a thing decides who may know it

misconceptions.statement: The 3-digit CVV and the card PIN can be shared if I am also sharing the card number, because they are the same kind of information.
misconceptions.why: Students treat all card numbers as just numbers printed or set for the card.
misconceptions.fix: The PIN, CVV, OTP and password are secret codes that must never be shared with anyone. Together with the card number they let others take money.

probe.question: A caller asks only for your CVV 'to cancel a wrong charge'. Is that okay?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, CVV is only a small number on the card.

misconceptions.root_belief: short or small things carry little risk

misconceptions.statement: To receive money by UPI I must enter my PIN, so a person asking me to enter my PIN to get a refund is correct.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up the actions of paying and receiving, as both use the same app screens.
misconceptions.fix: You enter the UPI PIN only to send money, never to receive it. If a request asks for a PIN to give you money, it is a scam.

probe.question: A buyer says: scan this QR and enter your PIN to receive Rs 2,000. Should you?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the PIN is needed to receive money.

misconceptions.root_belief: two similar actions work the same way

misconceptions.statement: If a website shows a padlock sign or starts with https, it is surely genuine and safe.
misconceptions.why: Safety lessons mention the padlock as a good sign, so it is taken as complete proof.
misconceptions.fix: A padlock only means the connection is encrypted, and fake sites can have it too. Check the full address spelling and use official apps or sites.

probe.question: A fake-looking bank site has a padlock. Is it safe to enter details?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the padlock shows it is genuine.

misconceptions.root_belief: one good sign proves something fully safe
misconceptions.source_hint: cybersecurity user-awareness studies on misreading padlock and https indicators

misconceptions.statement: To check if a call is genuine, I should call back the number given by the caller or in the message.
misconceptions.why: Calling back feels like a proper check, so students assume it works.
misconceptions.fix: The number given by the scammer leads to the scammer. Find the real number on your card, passbook or the bank's official website.

probe.question: A message says call 98xxxxxx to confirm your bank alert. How do you verify it?
probe.wrong_answer: Call that number and ask if it is real.

misconceptions.root_belief: checking with the same source gives proof

misconceptions.statement: A scheme with a nice office, ID cards and a certificate is a registered, legal investment.
misconceptions.why: Students link buildings, papers and staff to legitimacy.
misconceptions.fix: Check that the company or adviser is registered with a regulator such as SEBI or RBI on its official website. Offices and certificates can be faked.

probe.question: A firm has a big office and a certificate. Is that enough to trust its deposit scheme?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a real office means it is legal.

misconceptions.root_belief: looking professional means being legitimate

misconceptions.statement: Cyber fraud can only be reported by going to a police station, and 1930 is for other emergencies.
misconceptions.why: Students link all crime reporting only with the police station and general emergency numbers.
misconceptions.fix: Call the national cyber crime helpline 1930 or file a complaint at cybercrime.gov.in from home. You can also visit the police station.

probe.question: Someone has just cheated you of money by UPI. Which number or website can you use?
probe.wrong_answer: Only the police station; 1930 is not for this.

misconceptions.root_belief: one familiar route is the only route

misconceptions.statement: If the money is already gone, there is no use reporting, so I can wait and see.
misconceptions.why: Students feel transferred money cannot be traced or brought back.
misconceptions.fix: Reporting quickly, ideally within the first hours, helps banks and police freeze the money before it moves on. Waiting lowers the chance of getting it back.

probe.question: You lost money to a scam yesterday. Should you still report?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is already gone and cannot come back.

misconceptions.root_belief: what is done cannot be undone, so don't try

misconceptions.statement: If I tell the bank about the fraud it is enough, and I need not block my card or UPI myself.
misconceptions.why: Students think the bank will automatically do everything once told.
misconceptions.fix: Block the card, UPI and net banking at once through the bank helpline or app, change passwords, and also report on 1930. Both steps matter.

probe.question: Your card details were shared with a scammer. What steps should follow?
probe.wrong_answer: Just wait; the bank will fix it later.

misconceptions.root_belief: one step by one authority solves everything

misconceptions.statement: Only careless or foolish people get cheated, so I should hide it if it happens to me.
misconceptions.why: Students link fraud with stupidity and fear being blamed or laughed at.
misconceptions.fix: Scammers are skilled at tricking even educated and careful people. Telling a trusted adult and reporting quickly is the right and brave step.

probe.question: A friend lost money to a fake KYC call. What should they do?
probe.wrong_answer: Hide it, because only foolish people get cheated.

misconceptions.root_belief: bad things happen only to careless people
misconceptions.source_hint: research on victim blame and under-reporting of fraud
